turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Friday, September 18th. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex — and we're starting in The Hague, because a 25-year sentence just landed on a former head of state.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Hashim Thaçi, Kosovo's former president and KLA commander, was convicted Wednesday by the Kosovo Specialist Chambers — 25 years for murder, torture, and illegal detention.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the scale of the case — is this one incident or a pattern?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A pattern — the tribunal found 96 people killed, 303 tortured, 385 arbitrarily detained during and after the 1998-99 war. Three co-defendants got 25, 18, and 13 years.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How's it landing at home — is this seen as justice, or as an attack on the war of independence itself?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Split, hard — for many Kosovars, Thaçi is remembered as a liberation leader, so a war-crimes conviction against him reads to some as delegitimizing the whole independence struggle, which is exactly why the protests in Pristina turned angry rather than just sad.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And this is the man who was president as recently as 2020.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right — first head-of-state-level conviction to come out of the KLA's conduct, and it closes a case that's been central to how Kosovo tells its own founding story. There were angry protests in Pristina after the verdict.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Next — Yemen, where Washington is doing something unusual: saying no to Riyadh.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Saudi jets are hitting Yemen hard right now, and the Houthis claim they shot down a Saudi F-15 as they advance. Riyadh asked the Trump administration to join the strikes directly.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the US said no.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Declined — and it gets stranger. US officials secretly met Houthi representatives in Muscat over the weekend, and the Houthis pledged not to hit US or Israeli vessels in exchange.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So Washington's hedging between a core Gulf ally and quiet backchannel diplomacy with the group that ally is fighting.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly — and Saudi Arabia's air-defense stocks are thin enough that they're now asking France, the UK, Pakistan and Egypt for interceptor help. The UN says at least 9 children have been killed and over 57,000 people displaced in the last two weeks alone.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Third story — Germany's sending fighter jets to Latvia, but not for the reason you'd guess.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Four Eurofighter Typhoons plus troops, deploying for about a week in late September into early October — specifically to guard Latvian airspace ahead of the October 3rd parliamentary election.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Because of the drone incursions we've been hearing about from Russia and Belarus.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right, repeated incursions over recent weeks — this is the first time we've seen a NATO member specifically request air defense to protect an election process itself, not just general airspace. Riga's asking allies for more.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Back on Yemen for a second — how solid is that F-15 claim?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Genuinely unconfirmed — Riyadh hasn't acknowledged a loss, and the Houthis have a track record of overstating air-defense claims. What's not in dispute is the interceptor shortage driving Saudi Arabia to shop allies for help, and that's the more telling data point regardless of whether the jet claim holds up.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Onto US business — and a number that cuts against the "economy is struggling" story everyone's been telling.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Census Bureau's new release: real median household income hit $87,460 in 2025, up 2.6% year over year. Official poverty rate fell to 10.2% — a record low. Child poverty, 13.4% — also a record low.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That lands right after the Fed's first hike in three years.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which is the tension — the data behind the rate decision looks genuinely strong, not fragile, and that complicates any narrative that the Fed is tightening into weakness. The supplemental poverty measure was flat at 13.1%, for context.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does "record low poverty, still hiking rates" read as a policy win, or as the Fed being late?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Both, honestly — it vindicates the soft-landing case the Fed's been selling, but it also means this hike wasn't a rescue move, it was preemptive tightening into genuinely good numbers, which is exactly the kind of decision that gets second-guessed if growth rolls over next year.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second business story is smaller but sharper — the FTC just stepped into the gun industry.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Thursday, the FTC accepted a consent order over a stock-purchase deal between Beretta Holding and Sturm, Ruger and Company. It bars Beretta from placing board nominees on Ruger unless they're independent of Beretta.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So not blocking the investment, just the influence.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right — a fairly rare move, stopping interlocking-board control between two of the largest US gunmakers without going as far as challenging a full merger. The order doesn't touch the actual stock purchase, just governance — Beretta keeps its stake, it just can't put people on the Ruger board unless they're demonstrably independent of Beretta itself.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the FTC's drawing a line specifically around control, not ownership.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly the distinction — and it's a template worth watching, because it's a cheaper enforcement tool than a full merger challenge when the concern is influence rather than concentration.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: International — the Bank of Japan just made news of its own, this afternoon Tokyo time.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: BOJ hiked a quarter point to 1.25% — the highest level in 31 years. But it was a split vote, 7 to 2, with two board members dissenting.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the dissent about?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The dissenters doubt the case for continued tightening, and the market read that as a signal further hikes aren't a lock — the yen actually dropped on the decision, which is the opposite of what you'd expect from a hike on its face. A hawkish move that trades dovish because of how divided the committee looked.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the UK, the OBR just cut its 2026 growth forecast to 1.1% from 1.4%. Q3 GDP grew just 0.1%, partly because a JLR cyberattack shut down production and rippled through suppliers.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And Reeves already has a tough budget math problem.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It gets worse — day-to-day borrowing is running 10% higher year over year at £84 billion, and payrolls just saw the biggest two-month drop since late 2020, tied to her higher employer National Insurance contributions and the minimum wage increase. Growth, hiring, and borrowing all moving the wrong way at once makes her 2030 balanced-budget pledge look a lot harder to hit.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is the JLR shutdown a one-off shock or a sign of something more structural?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Mostly a one-off in isolation — a cyberattack halting a single automaker shouldn't move a national growth print this much on its own. But it's exposing how thin the UK's supplier-base resilience actually is; one company's outage rippling into a quarter-point of GDP is not a healthy amount of concentration risk.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the autumn budget just got a lot less forgiving.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Considerably — Reeves now needs a growth surprise or a borrowing surprise in her favor, and right now the data's handing her neither.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Markets actually had a real day yesterday — this isn't a "check the app" segment today.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's not. Wednesday's close was a genuine relief rally — the Nasdaq closed up 1.69%, which clears our bar for a real move. S&P up 1.14%, Dow up 0.61%.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: This is the day after the Fed's first hike in three years.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right, Wednesday itself was the sell-off — the 10-year briefly spiked above 5% intraday and stocks dropped. Thursday's session is the digestion: the 10-year eased back to 4.93%, down 7 basis points, and that gave tech room to run. Nvidia, Amazon, Qualcomm all up over 2%, Intel up 7%.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is that a real "the Fed isn't as scary as we thought" move, or just an oversold bounce?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Genuinely the more interesting question — a 25 basis point hike after three years of holding shouldn't have produced a spike through 5% on the 10-year in the first place. That tells you positioning was more fragile than the macro data justified. Thursday's bounce is the market re-pricing back toward what the actual economic backdrop — that strong Census income data we just covered — supports.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Anything else worth a number?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Gold's up 1.83% to $4,341 an ounce — real safe-haven demand still sitting alongside the equity rally, which is a bit of a tell that nobody's fully convinced this is over. Everything else — full index levels, PSEi, FX — it's all on the Markets tab. Peso's steady around 62.73.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: If you had to bet, does the relief rally hold into next week?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Cautiously — the Fed didn't signal a pause, just one hike, so the real test is whether the 10-year stays under 5% without more hawkish commentary. Gold not selling off alongside the equity bounce is the thing I'd watch most; that's the market keeping a hedge on.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Our deep dive today isn't markets or energy — it's the IMF, and something that happened very quietly two weeks ago.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Where's this from?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Adam Tooze's Chartbook newsletter, curating FT reporting — landed in the inbox last weekend. The IMF dropped Ricardo Reis, the LSE economist who was set to become its incoming chief economist and head of research, at the eleventh hour.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Dropped him why?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: He'd publicly criticized Trump's tariffs — warned they'd push up US consumer prices. Shortly after, the Fund installed Silvana Tenreyro instead. And separately, Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva dropped the Fund's gender and climate research focus after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pushed the IMF to stick to, quote, "core" macro-financial stability work.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is any of this actually confirmed, or is this FT sourcing doing a lot of work?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Fair to flag — there's no on-record confirmation from the IMF or from Reis himself. The FT's account rests on people familiar with the matter. So treat the specific mechanics as plausible, not proven.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: But the shape of it — an institution's research independence bending to its largest shareholder's informal pressure — that's the real story regardless of the details.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's exactly it. The chief economist post is supposed to be the Fund's independent technocratic voice — the body that writes the World Economic Outlook and the Article IV surveillance that anyone in markets treats as a baseline read on rates, capital flows, dollar liquidity. This isn't a formal vote-share exercise of US influence, it's informal leverage working on personnel.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What do we actually watch for, going forward?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Whether Tenreyro's research agenda — or the next WEO or Article IV language — visibly softens on tariff-inflation pass-through. That's the tell for whether this is cosmetic or a durable shift in how independent the Fund's forecasting actually is. If you're pricing Fed, dollar, or EM scenarios off IMF numbers, that's not a small thing to be quietly compromised.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Worth watching the next WEO release closely, then.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Very much so — mark your calendar. And there's a second reading of this worth sitting with: Bessent's push wasn't really about gender or climate research specifically, it was about narrowing what counts as the Fund's legitimate mandate at all.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Meaning the fight isn't over one economist's job, it's over what the IMF is even allowed to study.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right — and that's a much bigger stake than a single personnel decision. An institution that can be told which questions are "core" and which aren't has had its independence redefined, not just its staffing.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Has anything like this happened before at the Fund, or is this genuinely new territory?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: There's precedent for political pressure on IMF lending decisions — that's practically the Fund's whole history with its largest shareholders. What's less common is pressure aimed specifically at the research and forecasting side, the part that's supposed to be insulated because it's not disbursing anyone's money. That's the part of this that reads as a new kind of encroachment, not a repeat of an old one.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Energy — and there's a genuinely uncomfortable new number out of Pennsylvania.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: This one's from Utility Dive, Tuesday — the Pennsylvania PUC commissioned its own study of PJM's 2030 reliability under continued data-center load growth, independent of PJM's own capacity-auction modeling.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the answer wasn't good.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Worst case in the study: loss-of-load-expectation more than 100 times worse than PJM's own planning criterion — over 13 days a year with loss-of-load events, against a criterion of roughly one day in ten years. That's a state regulator's own number, not PJM's marketing.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's the kind of gap that changes how state commissions negotiate large-load tariffs.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly why it matters more than another capex headline. And it's not just Pennsylvania's problem — PJM covers 13 states plus DC, so an independent regulator producing a number this much worse than PJM's own criterion gives every other state commission in that footprint a credible basis to push back on PJM's self-reported margins too.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So this could reshape how the whole PJM footprint negotiates large-load interconnection, not just one state.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the read — and it lines up with IEA and BloombergNEF's own warnings this year that grid-planning timelines are structurally out of sync with hyperscaler procurement timelines. The planning criterion was built for a world of slow, predictable load growth; it was never stress-tested against a multi-gigawatt data-center campus showing up mid-cycle. Speaking of tariffs — Dominion and NextEra just proposed a roughly $1 billion a year Virginia large-load supplier program, a new state-specific mechanism, distinct from anything we've covered before.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's happening on the generation side while all this reliability anxiety builds?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Incumbent gas fleets are reshuffling, not expanding. Constellation bought Shell's 609-megawatt Rhode Island gas plant to grow its ISO-New England book. Same week, Shell turned around and bought a 169-megawatt Pennsylvania gas portfolio to grow its PJM position.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So existing dispatchable capacity is the scarce asset, not new builds.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right — everyone's trading the capacity that already exists toward the two grids under the most AI-load stress, PJM and ISO-NE, rather than betting on new construction timelines.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What about the behind-the-meter workaround — bypassing interconnection queues entirely?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Live example out of Texas — PUCT docket 59115. Hut 8, through its Silver Basin subsidiary, is trying to net-meter a 180-megawatt data center behind a 204-megawatt AC solar farm in Pecos County, sidestepping ERCOT's interconnection queue entirely.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And regulators are letting that happen?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: PUCT staff recommended approval on September 8th, subject to ERCOT conditions — but Texas-New Mexico Power filed adverse testimony, and the applicants filed a joint objection back on the 10th. Genuinely contested right now, real dollars, real precedent if it clears.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: On the financing side — anything moving on tax credits?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Yes, and it's a structural shift worth knowing. The clean-energy tax-credit market is oversupplied — production-linked credits are holding value, but investment tax credits are under real price pressure as corporate buyers gain leverage amid uncertainty over new federal transferability rules.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does that show up in an actual deal?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Suniva just closed an $835 million debt and equity raise — Goldman Sachs Alternatives and I Squared Capital — for its Laurens County, South Carolina solar cell plant, 4.5 gigawatts of capacity. But the schedule slip cost the plant one of its two full-output years at the full credit rate — timing against the step-down is now a live underwriting variable.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One more before we move on?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Excelsior Energy Capital sold a 625-megawatt AC Utah solar portfolio to Enel for $760 million — and the notable part is that Meta and Google are buying that output through utility tariffs, not corporate PPAs. Open question in the market right now on why hyperscalers are choosing tariff-based offtake over direct PPAs in some deals.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And there's a ratepayer-protection thread still unwinding in New Mexico?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Yes — TXNM had to unwind a Blackstone stock sale after a court ruled it illegal, and New Mexico's DOJ is now pressing for more information on whether costs from that ownership structure got passed indirectly to PNM ratepayers. It's a slower-burning story, but it's the clearest live test right now of how much scrutiny private-equity ownership of regulated utilities is actually going to face.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Zoom out for me before we move on.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Bloomberg's estimate: US data-center gas demand alone will overtake most countries' total gas demand by 2035. Every deal we just walked through is downstream of that one number.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tara, bago tayo pumunta sa Pilipinas, dalawang salita muna tayo — parehong may kinalaman sa mga balitang pang-negosyo ngayong araw.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Simulan natin sa "pagsasanib."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Pagsasanib" — ang ibig sabihin, ang pagsasama-sama ng dalawang kumpanya o entidad para maging isa. Pang-negosyo ang tono nito — madalas itong gamitin sa balitang pinansyal, hindi sa pang-araw-araw na usapan.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: May kaibhan ba ito sa "pagsasama" o "pakikipagsosyo"?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Oo — mas magaan ang "pagsasama," puwedeng tumukoy sa kahit anong pagbubuklod. Ang "pakikipagsosyo" naman, may nananatiling magkahiwalay na pagkakakilanlan ang dalawang panig. Ang "pagsasanib" ang pinakamatindi — halos mawawala na ang magkahiwalay na pagkatao ng isang kumpanya, sasanib ito nang tuluyan sa kabila.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Halimbawa?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Nagsasanib ang dalawang kumpanya para lumawak ang kanilang serbisyo." Gagamitin natin ito mamaya kapag pinag-usapan natin ang deal ng Grab.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Sige, susunod — "paglilitis."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Paglilitis" — ang proseso ng pagdinig at pagsusuri ng isang kaso sa hukuman. Legal at pormal ang rehistro nito — hindi ito ginagamit sa karaniwang usapan, kundi sa balitang pambatasan o pampulitika.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ano'ng pagkakaiba nito sa "imbestigasyon"?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ang imbestigasyon, panimulang pagsisiyasat pa lamang bago pa man dumating sa hukuman. Ang "paglilitis" naman, nasa yugto na kung saan opisyal nang nagsisimula ang pagdinig sa loob mismo ng korte, may mga ebidensiyang ipinapakita at pinagtatalunan.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Halimbawa naman ng gamit?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Nagsimula na ang paglilitis matapos ang kanyang pagdeklara ng 'hindi guilty.'" Gagamitin din natin ito sa susunod na segment.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Bago tayo lumipat — mayroon bang pagkakaiba sa dating ng dalawang salita, isa'y pang-negosyo, isa'y pambatas?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Oo — ang "pagsasanib" ay may positibong o neutral na dating, tungkol ito sa paglago at pagpapalawak. Ang "paglilitis" naman ay may seryosong timbang — laging nakaugnay sa pananagutan at hustisya. Kapag pinagsabay mo sa isang balita, madaling makita kung gaano kalawak ang saklaw ng usapang pang-ekonomiya at pampulitika ngayong araw.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Nagsasanib ang Grab at ang fintech na Atome Financial mula Singapore — bibilhin ng Grab ang 60 porsiyento ng Atome sa halagang 1.49 bilyong dolyar, cash, kasama na ang 260 milyong dolyar na bagong growth capital.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ang natitirang 40 porsiyento, kailan bibilhin?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Sa loob ng humigit-kumulang dalawang taon. Umaabot sa 25 milyong gumagamit ang Atome sa Pilipinas at apat pang bansa sa Timog-Silangang Asya — pinakamalaking pagsasanib sa fintech sa rehiyon ngayong taon.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: In English for a second — this makes Grab's play clear: it's betting its super-app moat on consumer lending, not just rides and delivery. Closing's expected Q3 2027, pending regulatory approval.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Meanwhile — the BSP question that's been hanging over the market all week just got answered. The Fed hiked 25 basis points to 3.75 to 4%, and the BSP is signaling it will NOT match with an off-cycle move.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Bakit hindi kailangang tumugon agad ang BSP?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Dahil hawak pa rin ng BSP ang positibong rate differential — mananatili itong nangunguna kaysa sa Fed rate, kaya may puwang pang maghintay hanggang sa naka-iskedyul na Oktubre meeting.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the peso reflects that confidence — closed around 62.73 to the dollar Wednesday, steadying off its intraday low, PSEi back above 5,900.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's a genuinely disciplined call — plenty of emerging-market central banks would have felt pressure to match a Fed hike defensively, and the BSP's basically saying the differential cushion is wide enough that it doesn't need to.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does that hold if the peso weakens again before October?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the real test — the BSP's credibility here rests on the cushion actually being wide enough to absorb a few weeks of volatility without flinching. If the peso slides meaningfully before the scheduled meeting, the "no off-cycle move" position gets a lot harder to defend.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Sa larangan naman ng batas — nagsimula na ang paglilitis kay dating Speaker Martin Romualdez matapos ang kanyang "hindi guilty" na plea noong Martes.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the actual next step in the courtroom?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Sandiganbayan's Third Division began pre-marking evidence today, running through September 24th. Romualdez's camp is now filing for bail — and separately, the court gave him 10 days to explain why he shouldn't be preventively suspended while the trial proceeds.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So this is the first real test of whether the 7.44 billion peso plunder case actually gets to trial, or stalls out on bail and suspension motions.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly the tension to watch over the next two weeks. Weather's quiet — just a weak low-pressure area off Palawan, no signal — and the PSEi move was routine, so we'll leave both there.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two Mandarin words today, both built for the China story coming up — a land auction that just fell apart.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: First word: 万一, wànyī. It means "in case" or "what if" — a connective for a hypothetical, often unwelcome, scenario. Register-wise it's flexible — used in both spoken and written Mandarin, but it signals real concern, not idle speculation like 也许.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How's it different from 如果?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 如果 is neutral — "if X happens." 万一 carries a worried undertone — "in the unlikely but concerning case that X happens." You'd use it for a risk you're actually hedging against, not a plain hypothetical.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Example: 万一土地拍卖再次流拍，地方政府的财政压力会更大。("In case the land auction fails again, local governments' fiscal pressure will get even worse.")

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second word — 财政缺口, cáizhèng quēkǒu.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Fiscal gap" or "fiscal shortfall" — a formal, written-register term, 书面语, straight out of financial and policy reporting. You wouldn't use this casually — it's desk language.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Any near-synonym worth contrasting?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 赤字, chìzì, is the closer everyday word — "deficit," often for a budget line. 财政缺口 is broader and more structural — it points to an underlying shortfall in capacity to fund obligations, not just one year's red ink. It collocates with words like 弥补, "to make up the gap," or 扩大, "to widen."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Example: 卖地收入下降，扩大了地方政府的财政缺口。("Falling land-sale revenue has widened local governments' fiscal gap.") We'll hear both of these again in a moment.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 万一买家不再出现，土地市场就会彻底停摆。("In case buyers stop showing up altogether, the land market grinds to a complete halt.") And that's not hypothetical anymore — it basically just happened in Beijing.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What happened?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A Beijing land parcel worth over a billion dollars drew interest from three developers ahead of the auction — but on auction day, only one showed up. Regulators scrapped the sale outright. No new date set.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is this a one-off, or part of something bigger?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Bigger — this follows late-August rules forcing "completed-home-only" presales, which cut land area sold 36% week-over-week across 70 major cities. First-half 2026 national land-sale revenue fell 31.5% year over year, the steepest same-period drop in nearly a decade.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And land sales are how local governments actually fund themselves.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which is the trap — 卖地收入下降，扩大了地方政府的财政缺口。Falling land-sale revenue is widening local governments' fiscal gap, right as they're relying on land sales to fund the debt swaps meant to fix that same fiscal hole.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the fix and the funding source for the fix are the same shrinking thing.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly — a debt-deflation squeeze that's feeding itself, and it's the same instrument, land, breaking on both ends at once.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 万一这种情况持续下去，地方政府只能靠更多借贷来填补财政缺口了。("In case this situation continues, local governments will have no choice but to rely on more borrowing to fill the fiscal gap.")

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 说得对。("Well said.") And that's the real risk here: borrowing to cover a shortfall caused by a financing model that's stopped working isn't a fix, it just moves the debt-deflation problem from the land market into the bond market.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Arts today leads with a show that opens tomorrow in Beijing — and it's a first for the artist.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: UCCA Center for Contemporary Art opens John Baldessari's first-ever exhibition in China on September 19th, running through January 3rd. Baldessari's a foundational figure in American conceptualism — died in 2020 — and this is a full five-decade survey.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What does the survey actually cover?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Early text-and-image experiments and the playful video work from the 1970s, through his cinematic photo-montages in the '80s, his later psychological work on perception, and the austere late pieces revisiting color, absence, and space. It's been years in development.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why has it taken this long for Baldessari to get a China show at all?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's really the story here — a genuinely canonical figure in Western conceptual art, and this is the first time a Chinese institution has done a proper survey of his work. Says as much about UCCA's expanding ambitions as it does about the belated recognition itself.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A second visual-art item worth a line: the 16th Gwangju Biennale opened September 5th, directed by Ho Tzu Nyen, titled "You Must Change Your Life," with 43 participating teams — timed against the close of Frieze Seoul and Kiaf's 25th-anniversary edition.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: On to classical — anything from the Gramophone Awards?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The 2026 shortlist just came out — 66 recordings across 11 categories, ceremony October 7th in London. Notable names: violinist Isabelle Faust and harpsichordist Kristian Bezuidenhout both shortlisted.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And literature?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The National Book Award Fiction longlist dropped this week — 10 titles out of 451 submissions, including a new queer epic from Marlon James and a story collection from Louise Erdrich. Finalists announced October 6th, winners November 18th.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Strong week for fiction, then.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Genuinely — worth putting a few of those on the list before the finalists narrow it down.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the actual case for leading with Kusama over everything else this week?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Scale and timing together — "biggest-ever" for a museum with the Stedelijk's history is a real claim, not marketing copy, and doing it as a posthumous tribute barely a month after her death gives the show a different emotional register than a standard career survey. The never-before-shown-in-Europe works are the reason to actually go, not just read about it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Op-eds — and Matthew Yglesias picked a fight with OpenAI this week.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: In Slow Boring, Yglesias argues OpenAI staff should actively oppose the company's own backing of "Leading the Future," a PAC built to chill federal AI regulation — and that Congress should hold real hearings on AI risk now, before that window closes.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Steelman it for me.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The steelman's solid — a company funding an anti-regulation PAC while its own safety researchers are sounding alarms internally is a genuine conflict of interest, and it's fair to say that shouldn't go unremarked.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the counter?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Congress should hold hearings" is about the lowest-stakes ask available in Washington — hearings generate soundbites, not statute. Yglesias doesn't offer a real theory of how a gridlocked Congress turns that concern into binding rules before the midterms eat the calendar.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: We've got a second one in reserve if you want a different angle.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: We do — Noah Smith's "The anti-American Right," using Texas Railroad Commissioner nominee Bo French's anti-immigrant tweet firestorm to argue the New Right increasingly treats nonwhite immigrants and their US-born children as permanent outsiders. Steelman: it documents a real rhetorical shift among elected Republicans, not just online trolls. Counter: one primary winner's tweet is a thin reed for a sweeping "the Right has changed" thesis.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Both worth sitting with — but the AI-regulation one is the sharper hook this week.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: On the Smith piece specifically — the useful part isn't the Bo French tweet itself, it's the framing question underneath it: is "assimilationism" actually the historical norm the piece assumes, or is Smith reading a fairly recent post-1965 consensus back onto the whole conservative tradition?

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the counter-take on that one cuts even deeper than "one tweet is a thin reed."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It does — if the baseline he's measuring deviation from is itself contested, the whole "this is new" argument gets shakier, not just the sample size.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does the Yglesias piece have the same weakness — is he assuming a baseline that might not hold either?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Less so — his ask is concrete enough to test: did Congress hold hearings or didn't it, is OpenAI still funding the PAC or did it pull back. That's falsifiable in a way "the Right has changed" isn't, which is actually the strongest argument for treating it as the sharper piece this week, independent of whether you agree with the policy conclusion.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: We'll close in Henrico, Virginia, with a chef named Andrew Griffin.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What happened?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Griffin, who runs Deep Run Roadhouse, was outside his not-yet-open new location when he found an elderly regular — everyone calls her Miss Duke — stranded after a senior-transport drop-off went wrong.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And he didn't just call someone else to handle it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: He drove her home himself. Then, thinking about his own grandmother, he made sure her fridge was actually stocked before he left — no fanfare, nobody asking him to.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Did anyone catch it?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Local TV did, and surprised him afterward with a kindness award and $300 — but that was never the point for him. He said he just thought about his own grandmother needing the same thing someday, and that was the whole decision.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Clean story, no caveat needed.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: None at all — exactly the kind of thing worth carrying into your weekend.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's The Morning Commute for Friday, September 18th.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Have a good one — we'll see you tomorrow.
